title: Beni: the stages of life
hookLine: Beni traces a life from the womb to old age, forgetting the Lord at each stage (Sri Rag, Beni, ang 93)

lines: A BOX OF PHOTOS ON THE TABLE.
cards: A box of family photos, tipped out on a table. A baby in a hospital blanket. A kid with a scraped knee and a grin.
A teenager trying hard to look bored. A wedding. A gray head bent over a grandchild.
Shuffle them into order and you have a whole life in a few minutes. Beni, one of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib, lays out a life like that in a hymn, from the womb to old age.
And in every snapshot, something is missing.

teach.b: The hymn is in Sri Raag, on Ang 93, and it starts somewhere surprising: before birth. In paraphrase: O man, when you were in the womb, upside down, you were absorbed in remembering, with no pride in your body.
Then you were born, and you forgot. Next, childhood: caught up in play and sweets, the Lord slips from mind.

teach.h: CHILD, YOUTH, OLD AGE: EACH ONE FORGETS.
teach.b: Then youth: the body is strong, the eye wanders after pleasure and money, and pride grows. Then old age: the hair goes white, the body weakens, and there's regret, but now it's hard to change course.
Each stage has its own reason to forget. The child is too busy. The young adult is too sure.
The old one is too tired. Beni isn't mocking any of them. Forgetting doesn't belong to one bad season of life; it comes along to every one.

Then he signs off with a hard question, in paraphrase: says Beni, listen, devotees, who has ever found liberation after death? That's the turn. If freedom doesn't come after death, it has to come in one of these photos.
Sikh teaching speaks of being free while still alive, here, in the middle of an ordinary life.
Read that way, the hymn points to the photo you're in right now, the stage you're standing in, with its own reason to forget, as the place to remember.

how: Beni's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching speaks of jivan mukti, being free while still alive, through remembering the Name in everyday life.

o: a poet who praised the joys of youth and strength
a sage who taught that freedom comes after death
the Bhagat who sang of forgetting at every age

p: caught up in play and sweets

s: it begins before birth, in the womb, where he says the soul was absorbed in remembering.
Beni says only the young forget
every stage forgets: the child, the young adult and the old.
the hymn ends by asking who was freed after death
says Beni: listen, devotees, who has found liberation after death?

games.q: you're Beni, and you've shown forgetting at every stage of a life. how do you end the hymn?
o: with a promise of freedom after death.
with a question: who was ever freed after death?
with a list of rules for old age.
games.why: he ends with the question. if no one is freed after death, the remembering has to happen in this life, at this stage.

practice: Find yourself in Beni's photos: busy like the child, sure like the young, tired like the old, or somewhere between.
Name your stage's own reason to forget, honestly and without blame, and then just breathe, remembering right where you are. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath.

wordCard.voice: Beni. The Bhagat of Sri Raag who lays out a life from the womb to old age, finds forgetting in every stage, and asks who was ever freed after death.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the Bhagat's name as it appears in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: remember at every stage. Every stage has room for it, this one included. Seven hundred eighty-one days now.

sources.ref: Sri Raag, Beni (re nar garabh kundal jab aachhat), Ang 93
